title: How Much Local Data Does a Malaria Parasite Counter Need in a New Country? A Three-Country Study of Thick-Smear Microscopy
content: Automated parasite counting on thick blood smears could support malaria diagnosis where trained microscopists are scarce, but detectors are usually trained and tested on images from a single site. We train a YOLO11 detector for parasites and white blood cells (WBCs) on smartphone microscopy from Bangladesh and evaluate it on public thick-smear datasets from Ghana and Tanzania. At the training site, parasite density estimated with the standard WBC method is within a median 12% of the expert count on 30 unseen patients (95% CI 7–16%). In a country never seen in training, parasite detection falls from 0.81–0.90 mAP50 to 0.11–0.33, and per-image counts fail in opposite directions: 2.8 times too many parasites in Tanzania and about one sixth of the true number in Ghana. Training on two countries does not improve performance on a third, and re-tuning the confidence threshold on local data leaves median count errors near 60%. Fine-tuning on 25 labelled local images recovers about 80% of the lost detection accuracy, and with 50 images per-image counting error matches that of a model trained on all available local data (21% vs 22% in Tanzania; 12% vs 9% in Ghana). In Tanzania, the unadapted model's errors are concentrated in the blurriest images. We also document two silent data pitfalls, inconsistent image orientation metadata and differing magnification across datasets. The results suggest that sites adopting such tools should budget for labelling a small local set rather than relying on a model validated elsewhere.
